title: What to Do If Youre Layered in an Organization
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes being 'layered' — having a new manager inserted between you and your former boss — as something more nuanced than an automatic demotion. It walks through the two most common causes: genuine performance concerns versus a leader simply having too many direct reports to manage well. The piece argues most layering actually falls into the second category and can be a hidden benefit, giving the layered person more attentive mentorship. It ends by urging anyone who's been layered to get a direct, honest answer about the reason before deciding how to respond.
points: Layering means a new leader is inserted between you and the person you used to report to.
One cause is performance-related demotion; the far more common cause is a leader simply having too many direct reports.
Leaders with more than 10 direct reports face a real choice about how to give everyone adequate attention.
Being layered for span-of-control reasons often means gaining a more attentive, hands-on manager.
The key first step is having a frank conversation to understand the actual reason for the change.
quotes: Being “layered” in an organization means reporting to someone who now sits between you and the leader you used to report to.
While a recasting of reporting lines due to performance is not unusual, it is not the most common reason for layering.
The number one reason leaders and team members are layered is because their leader has too many direct reports.
In the best cases, this actually turns out to be a hugely positive outcome, as the layered party now has the resources and guidance to get more done with the right amount of oversight.
Having a frank conversation with the powers that be is in everyone’s best interest.
